extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduates, graduate students, and researchers in algebraic topology
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition and foundational results connecting generalized cohomology theories with ordinary cohomology, constructions and properties of fibrations and homotopy fibers, loopspaces, Postnikov and Moore–Postnikov towers, and related constructions (pathspace, pullback).

rubrics_metrics.name: Naturality of isomorphism between h^*(X) and H^*(X; G)
rubrics_metrics.description: The cellular chain complexes for h_*(X) and H_*(X; G) are isomorphic, giving isomorphisms h_n(X) ≈ H_n(X; G) for all n; these isomorphisms are natural with respect to maps f: X → Y once f is deformed to be cellular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To verify naturality, deform f to a cellular map so it takes each pair (X^n, X^{n-1}) to (Y^n, Y^{n-1}) and induces the same cellular chain map in both theories; passage to quotient maps X^n/X^{n-1}→Y^n/Y^{n-1} reduces to maps S^n_α→S^n_β whose degrees determine induced maps on h_n, hence the cellular chain maps agree and the isomorphism is natural.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling infinite cells in cohomology (finitely supported coboundary maps)
rubrics_metrics.description: For cohomology theories the cellular cochain groups are direct products (one copy of G per cell), so when there are infinitely many cells in a dimension, one must check that cellular coboundary maps are determined by finitely supported maps because attaching maps have compact image meeting only finitely many lower-dimensional cells.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decompose the domain product into a finite supported part and the remainder on which the map is zero; finitely supported maps are determined by their restrictions to the G factors, which ensures the cellular coboundary maps in the generalized theory agree with those in ordinary cohomology and gives naturality of isomorphisms H^n(X;G)≈h(X,K(G,n)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Representability: H^n(X; G) ≈ [X, K(G,n)] (fundamental class existence)
rubrics_metrics.description: The functors h^n(X) = [X, K(G,n)] define a reduced cohomology theory whose coefficient groups agree with H^n(S^i; G), so there are natural isomorphisms T: h(X,K(G,n)) → H^n(X; G) for all CW complexes X; in particular the element α = T(11) ∈ H^n(K(G,n); G) is the fundamental class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a CW model K for K(G,n) with (n−1)-skeleton a point; the identity 1 ∈ h^n(K) corresponds under cellular identification to the inclusion of the n-skeleton and yields α by T(11). Naturality gives T([f]) = f^*(α) for any f: X→K(G,n), so cohomology classes arise as pullbacks of the universal class α.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description of the fundamental class as a cellular cocycle
rubrics_metrics.description: The fundamental class α ∈ H^n(K(G,n); G) is represented by the cellular cocycle assigning to each n-cell the element of the coefficient group G = π_n(K) given by the inclusion of the cell's closure into K.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For a cellular map f: X→K, the corresponding element of H^n(X; G) is represented by the cocycle sending each n-cell of X to the element of G represented by composing f with a characteristic map for that cell.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of cup product via smash product and µ
rubrics_metrics.description: Given maps f: X→K_m and g: Y→K_n, define the cross product and compose Km∧Kn → K_{m+n} by a map µ inducing multiplication on π_{m+n}; this yields cup (and cross) products in cohomology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The map µ: Km ∧ Kn → K_{m+n} is chosen so it induces the multiplication R⊗R→R on π_{m+n} (or on H_{m+n} via Hurewicz and Künneth). For R=Z one can realize µ by extending the inclusion S^m ∧ S^n = S^{m+n} into Km+n. Standard properties of cup product (e.g. graded-commutativity) follow from this construction; the sign (−1)^{mn} appears from switching factors of Sm ∧ S^n.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of fibration (homotopy lifting property)
rubrics_metrics.description: A fibration p: E → B is a map having the homotopy lifting property with respect to all spaces (i.e., lifts exist for homotopies into B starting from lifts at time zero).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish fibrations from fiber bundles: in a fiber bundle fibers are homeomorphic, but fibrations only give homotopy-theoretic control; many constructions (pullbacks, pathspace) produce fibrations from arbitrary maps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fibers over a path-component are homotopy equivalent (Prop. 4.61)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a fibration p: E → B, the fibers F_b = p^{-1}(b) over points in the same path-component of B are all homotopy equivalent; a path γ yields a homotopy equivalence L_γ: F_{γ(0)}→F_{γ(1)} with properties: (a) homotopic paths give homotopic L_γ; (b) composition of paths corresponds to composition of L_γ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct L_γ by lifting the homotopy g_t: F_{γ(0)}→B defined by g_t(F_{γ(0)}) = γ(t); use the homotopy lifting property and check the two listed properties to deduce L_γ is a homotopy equivalence with inverse from the inverse path.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local fiber-homotopy triviality over locally contractible bases
rubrics_metrics.description: If B is locally contractible, any fibration p: E → B is locally fiber-homotopy equivalent to a projection U×F → U (i.e., locally fiber-homotopically trivial).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use pullback and local contractibility to find neighborhoods U where p^{-1}(U)→U is fiber-homotopy equivalent to a product fibration; fiber-preserving maps and fiber homotopy equivalence are the correct notions of equivalence for fibrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pullback fibration and homotopy invariance (Prop. 4.62)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a fibration p: E → B and a homotopy f_t: A → B, the pullback fibrations f_0^*(E) → A and f_1^*(E) → A are fiber homotopy equivalent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form the pullback F = F^*(E) for the homotopy F: A×I→B and view the restricted fibrations over A×{0} and A×{1}; construct fiber-preserving maps via lifted homotopies as in Proposition 4.61.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fibration over a contractible base is product up to fiber homotopy (Corollary 4.63)
rubrics_metrics.description: A fibration E→B with contractible base B is fiber homotopy equivalent to the product fibration B×F→B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pullback via the identity and a constant map; use Proposition 4.62 to show the original fibration is fiber-homotopy equivalent to the product.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pathspace construction: factor any map as homotopy equivalence followed by a fibration (Prop. 4.64)
rubrics_metrics.description: For any map f: A → B, define E_f = {(a, γ) | a ∈ A, γ: I→B, γ(0) = f(a)} with p(a,γ) = γ(1); then p: E_f → B is a fibration and A includes into E_f as constant-paths, giving a factorization A → E_f → B where A→E_f is a homotopy equivalence and E_f→B is a fibration. The fiber of p is the homotopy fiber of f.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Topologize E_f as a subspace of A×B^I with compact-open topology; construct lifts by concatenating existing path-coordinate with the homotopy trace; observe E_f deformation retracts onto the constant-path inclusion of A.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation of homotopy fiber to relative homotopy groups
rubrics_metrics.description: If f: A→B is the inclusion of a subspace, the homotopy fiber F_f identifies π_{i+1}(B,A,x_0) with π_i(F_f, γ_0), relating long exact sequences of a pair and of the associated fibration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use identification of maps (I^{i+1}, ∂I^{i+1}, J^i)→(B,A,x_0) with maps (I^i, ∂I^i)→(F_f, γ_0) to deduce the isomorphism of homotopy groups and identification of long exact sequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Loopspace as fiber of path fibration and consequence for homotopy groups
rubrics_metrics.description: For basepoint inclusion, E_f = P B (paths starting at basepoint), p: P B→B has fiber the loopspace ΩB; since P B is contractible, the long exact sequence gives π_n(B,x_0) ≈ π_{n-1}(ΩB,x_0) for all n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use contractibility of P B (deform paths by truncation) and the path fibration exact sequence to identify homotopy groups shifted by one via loopspace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion E → E^p is a fiber homotopy equivalence; homotopy fibers ≃ actual fibers (Prop. 4.65)
rubrics_metrics.description: If p: E→B is already a fibration, then the inclusion E → E^p (pathspace construction applied to p) is a fiber homotopy equivalence; thus homotopy fibers of p are homotopy equivalent to the actual fibers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply homotopy lifting to a contraction-of-paths homotopy on E^p producing fiber-preserving homotopies that show the inclusion has a fiber-preserving homotopy inverse up to fiber homotopy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contractible total space implies fiber ≃ loopspace (Prop. 4.66)
rubrics_metrics.description: If F→E→B is a fibration (or fiber bundle) with E contractible, then there is a weak homotopy equivalence F → ΩB.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose a contraction of E with p to obtain a map E→P B, restrict to F to get F→ΩB and compare long exact sequences (five-lemma) to deduce weak equivalence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iterated homotopy fibers and Puppe sequence (fibration sequence / fiber sequences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Iterating homotopy-fiber construction yields a (Puppe) sequence ··· → Ω^2 B → ΩF → ΩE → ΩB → F → E → B where any two consecutive maps form a fibration up to homotopy and leftward terms are loopings of later maps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe the actual constructions: homotopy fiber of inclusion F→E is related to loopspace ΩB, squares commute up to homotopy, and long exact sequences for any fibration in the sequence coincide with that of F→E→B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Postnikov tower definition and properties
rubrics_metrics.description: A Postnikov tower for a path-connected X is a diagram X → ··· → X_n → X_{n-1} → ··· where (1) X→X_n induces isomorphism on π_i for i ≤ n, (2) π_i(X_n) = 0 for i > n, and (3) by converting maps to fibrations one can arrange X_n→X_{n-1} to be a fibration with fiber K(π_n X, n).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct by successively converting maps to fibrations; the fibers are Eilenberg–MacLane spaces and the X_n are (up to homotopy) twisted products of K(π_n X, n). Postnikov stages are useful to study homotopy/homology in finite ranges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inverse limit of fibrations and lim, lim^1 exact sequence (Prop. 4.67)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a sequence of fibrations ··· → X_2 → X_1, the natural map π_i(lim X_n) → lim π_i(X_n) is surjective; it is injective provided maps π_{i+1}(X_n) → π_{i+1}(X_{n-1}) are surjective for large n. There is a natural exact sequence 0 → lim^1 π_{i+1}(X_n) → π_i(lim X_n) → lim π_i(X_n) → 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct coordinate maps and use homotopy lifting to adjust representatives so projections match; the kernel is described by lim^1 of the next homotopy groups. For Postnikov towers this gives X ≃ weakly lim X_n.

rubrics_metrics.name: k-invariants and principal fibrations for building Postnikov towers
rubrics_metrics.description: If the fibrations in a Postnikov tower are principal (i.e., each X_{n+1} is, up to weak equivalence, the homotopy fiber of a map k_n: X_n → K(π_{n+1}X, n+2)), then the classes k_n ∈ H^{n+2}(X_n; π_{n+1}X) (the k-invariants) specify how to build X inductively from Eilenberg–MacLane spaces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When all k_n = 0, X is (up to weak equivalence) the product ∏ K(π_n X, n); in general X is a 'twisted product' determined by the k-invariants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for existence of principal Postnikov tower (Theorem 4.69)
rubrics_metrics.description: A connected CW complex X has a Postnikov tower of principal fibrations iff π_1(X) acts trivially on π_n(X) for all n > 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interprets principal fibrations as requiring trivial action of π_1 on higher homotopy groups; the proof identifies the action on π_n(X) with the action on π_{n+1}(X_{n-1}, X_n) and applies Lemma 4.70.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma on CW pair being equivalent to a fibration pair (Lemma 4.70)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let (X,A) be a connected CW pair whose homotopy fiber of the inclusion A ↪ X is a K(π, n) with n ≥ 1. Then there exists a fibration F→E→B and a map (X,A)→(E,F) inducing weak homotopy equivalences X→E and A→F iff the action of π_1(A) on π_{n+1}(X,A) is trivial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the action is trivial, relative Hurewicz gives π_{n+1}(X,A) ≈ H_{n+1}(X,A) and one can form X/A and attach higher cells to build K(π,n+1); converting the associated map to a fibration produces the desired fibration pair and the five-lemma on long exact sequences gives weak equivalences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moore–Postnikov tower for a map f: X→Y (existence and uniqueness, Theorem 4.71)
rubrics_metrics.description: For any map f between connected CW complexes there exists a Moore–Postnikov tower Z_n with X → ··· → Z_n → Z_{n-1} → ··· → Y such that (1) X→Z_n induces isomorphism on π_i for i < n and surjection for i=n, (2) Z_n→Y induces isomorphism on π_i for i>n and injection for i=n, and (3) Z_{n+1}→Z_n is a fibration with fiber K(π_n F, n) where F is the homotopy fiber of f. The tower is unique up to homotopy; principal towers exist iff π_1(X) acts trivially on π_n(M_f,X) for n>1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct Z_n via Propositions 4.17/4.18 applied to the mapping cylinder M_f, convert maps to fibrations inductively, and use homotopy lifting to make triangles strictly commutative; principal condition parallels the Postnikov case using action of π_1 on relative homotopy groups.
